sections.b: Deuteronomy 12 sets the rule that shapes the whole law code: "seek out the place the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name there." Burnt offerings, tithes, firstborn animals, vows and the three pilgrim feasts all go there (12:5–14; 14:23; 15:20; 16:2, 6, 11, 15–16). Because worship moved to one place, the law also allows meat to be slaughtered and eaten in every town without an altar (12:15, 20–22), lets the tithe be turned into silver for the journey (14:24–26), and sends hard court cases to the chosen place (17:8). The phrase "to make his name live there" keeps God's own dwelling in heaven (26:15). The place is never named, which let Jews read it as Jerusalem and Samaritans as Mount Gerizim.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 12:1–28; Deuteronomy 14:23–26; Deuteronomy 16:1–17; Deuteronomy 17:8–10; Deuteronomy 26:2, 15; 1 Kings 8:29; 2 Kings 23:1–25; John 4:20–24

common: Most scholars connect this law with King Josiah's reform of 622 BC, which closed the local shrines (2 Kings 23).
uncommon: Some argue that "the place" originally meant any place God chose in turn, such as Shiloh, Shechem and finally Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:12).

claude.title: Why leave it unnamed?
claude.body: I think the silence is deliberate and theological. A book set on the far side of the Jordan could not name Jerusalem without breaking its frame, but it also makes the choice belong to God, not to any city. When Jeremiah warns that the temple can become a den of robbers, he points to Shiloh, a place God once chose and then left (Jeremiah 7:12–14). The unnamed place is a promise, not a property deed. This overlaps with J. Gordon McConville's reading of the unnamed place as a sign that God remains free to choose.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 17:14–20 is the only law in the Torah about kings. It permits Israel to set a king over itself "like all the nations," but then makes him unlike them: he must be chosen by God and be a "brother," must not multiply horses, wives or silver and gold, and must write his own copy of the law and read it all his life, so that "his heart will not be lifted up above his brothers." The king has no duties in war or courts in this law; his main job is to obey. Solomon is later described as breaking each limit: horses from Egypt, many wives who turned his heart, and gold beyond counting (1 Kings 10:14–11:4).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 17:14–20; 1 Samuel 8:4–22; 1 Kings 10:14–11:4; 2 Kings 22:8–13; Psalm 72

common: Many readers see the law as a critique of Solomon, written or shaped with his reign in view.
uncommon: Bernard Levinson calls the passage an early "constitution" that puts the king under a written law shared with the people.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 16:18–20 sets up judges in every town and gives the rule in three short commands: "Do not bend justice. Do not play favorites. Do not take a bribe." The doubled word in "Justice, justice is what you must pursue" stresses the point. The code then adds the rule of two or three witnesses (17:6; 19:15), a higher court at the chosen place (17:8–13), punishment for false witnesses (19:16–21), the end of punishing children for parents' crimes (24:16), protection for foreigners, orphans and widows in court (24:17), a limit of forty blows (25:3) and honest weights (25:13–16). Exodus already warned that "a bribe blinds" (Exodus 23:8); Deuteronomy says it blinds even the wise.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 16:18–20; Deuteronomy 17:2–13; Deuteronomy 19:15–21; Deuteronomy 24:16–17; Deuteronomy 25:1–3, 13–16; Exodus 23:1–8; Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1

common: The rule of two or three witnesses became basic to Jewish law and is applied by Jesus and Paul to church discipline (Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1).

sections.b: Deuteronomy 15 holds two statements side by side: "there will be no one in need among you" if Israel obeys (15:4), and "there will never stop being people in need in the land" (15:11). The answer to the tension is a command: "Open your hand wide." The law releases debts every seventh year (15:1–11), sends freed slaves away with gifts (15:12–18), shares the third-year tithe (14:28–29; 26:12), returns a poor man's coat before night (24:12–13), pays day laborers before sundown (24:14–15) and leaves sheaves, olives and grapes for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow (24:19–22). Again and again the reason given is memory: "Remember that you were a slave in Egypt."
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 15:1–18; Deuteronomy 24:10–22; Deuteronomy 26:12–13; Mark 14:7; Luke 4:18; James 5:4

common: Jesus' saying "you have the poor among you at all times" (Mark 14:7) echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, whose next words command generosity.

claude.title: A law against the closed fist
claude.body: What strikes me in Deuteronomy 15 is that it legislates attitudes. It forbids a "worthless thought" about the coming release year and tells the lender not to resent giving (15:9–10). Laws normally govern deeds. This one aims at the heart that comes before the deed, which is why later readers found it so close to the teaching of Jesus. Many commentators, including Weinfeld and Tigay, make the same observation about the book's concern for inner attitude.

sections.b: Deuteronomy gathers the Torah's lending rules. Every seventh year is a "release" in which loans to a fellow Israelite are cancelled (15:1–3), and no one may refuse a loan because the release is near (15:9). Interest is forbidden to a "brother" but allowed to a foreigner (23:19–20), going beyond Exodus 22:25, which spoke of the poor. A lender may not take a millstone as a pledge, since it is "taking a life" (24:6), may not enter the borrower's house to choose a pledge (24:10–11), must return a poor man's coat by night (24:12–13), and may not take a widow's garment at all (24:17). In the first century, Hillel's prozbul let loans survive the release year by assigning them to a court, so that lenders would not stop lending (Mishnah Shevi'it 10:3–4).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 15:1–11; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Deuteronomy 24:6, 10–13, 17; Exodus 22:25–27; Leviticus 25:35–37; Nehemiah 5:1–13

common: The medieval church read these verses as a ban on all interest among Christians.
uncommon: Some modern readers argue the laws target exploitation of the poor, not commercial credit, as Calvin argued in 1545.

sections.b: In Deuteronomy 18 Moses forbids Israel's diviners, omen readers and necromancers, and then gives the alternative: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers. You must listen to him" (18:15). God promises to "put my words in his mouth" (18:18). The passage then gives a test for a false prophet: a prediction that does not come true (18:21–22), alongside the earlier test of a prophet who leads to other gods even with signs that come true (13:1–5). Peter and Stephen quote the promise about Jesus (Acts 3:22–23; 7:37), and the crowds ask whether John or Jesus is "the Prophet" (John 1:21; 6:14).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:9–22; Deuteronomy 34:10–12; John 1:21, 45; John 6:14; Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37

common: Christians have long read the promise as fulfilled in Jesus, the new lawgiver who speaks God's words.
Jewish tradition (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Maimonides) reads it as the promise of the line of true prophets after Moses, the basis of prophecy in Israel.
uncommon: Samaritans read it of a single coming figure, the Taheb, and some scholars, such as William Holladay, think Jeremiah was presented as the prophet like Moses.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 21:22–23 deals with the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree for display. It must be buried that same day, "for a man who is hanged is cursed by God," and leaving it would make the land unclean. Joshua took down the king of Ai and the five kings at sunset (Joshua 8:29; 10:26–27). The Hebrew phrase can also mean "an insult to God," since a human made in God's image is left disgraced, and the rabbis read it that way (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4). The Greek translation's "everyone who hangs on a tree" is the wording Paul uses (Galatians 3:13).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Joshua 8:29; Joshua 10:26–27; 2 Samuel 21:9–14; John 19:31; Acts 5:30; Acts 10:39; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24

common: Paul reads the verse to say that Christ took on the law's curse on behalf of others.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 26:1–11 gives the words a farmer speaks when he brings a basket of first fruits to the priest. He tells Israel's story in the first person: a wandering Aramean father, slavery in Egypt, a cry to God, rescue "with a strong hand," and the gift of "a land flowing with milk and honey." Then he says, "look, I have brought the first of the fruit of the ground that you, LORD, have given me." The gift becomes a confession of faith. The Mishnah tractate Bikkurim describes the joyful processions to Jerusalem in Second Temple times, and the Passover Haggadah builds its retelling of the exodus on these verses.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 26:1–11; Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:26; Leviticus 23:9–14; Numbers 18:12–13; 1 Corinthians 15:20–23

common: Many Christians see Christ's resurrection on the day after the Sabbath of Passover week as the fulfillment of the first sheaf (Leviticus 23:11; 1 Corinthians 15:20).

sections.b: Deuteronomy 20 gives rules for war. A priest encourages the army, and officials send home the man with a new house, an unharvested vineyard or a fiancée, and anyone afraid (20:1–9). A distant city is first offered peace; if it refuses, its men are killed and the rest taken as spoil (20:10–15). The cities of the seven nations, however, are to be put under the ban, "so that they will not teach you" their worship (20:16–18). Fruit trees must not be cut down in a siege (20:19–20). Chapter 21 adds rules protecting a captive woman (21:10–14), and 25:17–19 commands Israel to blot out the memory of Amalek. These laws raise some of the hardest moral questions in the Bible.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 20:1–20; Deuteronomy 21:10–14; Deuteronomy 23:9–14; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Judges 7:3; 1 Maccabees 3:55–56

common: Jewish tradition distinguished commanded wars against the seven nations and Amalek, now impossible to carry out, from optional wars that needed a court's approval (Mishnah Sotah 8:7).
uncommon: Some scholars argue that the ban laws were written long after the conquest as a rhetorical call to religious purity, not as a record of what happened.

sections.b: Deuteronomy's slave laws revise Exodus 21. A Hebrew slave, now explicitly "a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman," goes free in the seventh year and must not be sent away empty-handed, but loaded with flock, grain and wine (15:12–15). A slave who chooses to stay has his ear pierced at the door (15:16–17). A slave who escapes to Israel must not be handed back to his master (23:15–16), a sharp contrast with Hammurabi's laws. Kidnapping an Israelite to enslave or sell him is a capital crime (24:7). The reason given is memory: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (15:15).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 15:12–18; Deuteronomy 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 24:7, 18; Exodus 21:2–11, 16; Jeremiah 34:8–22; Philemon 10–16; 1 Timothy 1:10

common: Abolitionists cited Deuteronomy 23:15–16 against laws requiring the return of fugitive slaves.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 is the Torah's only passage on the process of divorce. It assumes a husband who finds "something indecent" in his wife, writes her a certificate, and sends her away, and it rules that if she marries again, he may never take her back. The Mishnah records how Shammai, Hillel and Akiva read "something indecent" (Mishnah Gittin 9:10), and the Pharisees' question to Jesus about divorce "for any cause" belongs to that debate (Matthew 19:3–9). Deuteronomy also protects wives in other ways: a new husband stays home a year to bring his wife joy (24:5), a man who slanders his bride loses the right to divorce her (22:19), and the unloved wife's son keeps the double share (21:15–17).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 21:15–17; Deuteronomy 22:13–30; Deuteronomy 24:1–5; Jeremiah 3:1–8; Malachi 2:14–16; Matthew 5:31–32; Matthew 19:3–9; Mark 10:2–12

common: Jesus treats the divorce law as a concession to hard hearts and grounds marriage in creation (Matthew 19:8).
uncommon: David Instone-Brewer argues that Jesus rejected only Hillel's "any cause" divorce, not other grounds the Torah allowed.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 25:5–10 is the only law of levirate marriage in the Torah. When brothers live together and one dies without a son, his widow must not marry outside the family; her husband's brother marries her, and the first son "will carry on the name of his dead brother." A brother who refuses is shamed at the town gate: the widow pulls off his sandal, spits in his face, and his family is called "the house of the man whose sandal was pulled off." Genesis 38 and the book of Ruth show versions of the custom in practice, and Jewish law still performs the sandal ceremony, chalitsah.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 25:5–10; Genesis 38:6–26; Ruth 4:1–17; Matthew 22:23–33

sections.b: Deuteronomy 14:3–21 repeats the clean-food list of Leviticus 11 more briefly, adding a list of ten clean wild and domestic animals (14:4–5) and leaving out most of the insects. It frames the list with identity: "You are children of the LORD your God" and "a people holy to the LORD your God" (14:1–2, 21). It also adds that an animal that died on its own may be given to the foreigner who lives in your towns or sold to a foreigner from another nation (14:21), and repeats "Do not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother" from Exodus 23:19 and 34:26. The bird list differs slightly from Leviticus; see the variant on 14:13.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 14:1–21; Leviticus 11:1–47; Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:26; Acts 10:9–16; Mark 7:19

sections.b: Deuteronomy's tithe differs from that of Numbers 18, where the tithe goes to the Levites. Here a tenth of grain, wine and oil is eaten by the farmer's household "before the LORD" at the chosen place, or turned into silver and spent there on "anything you want" (14:22–26). Every third year the tithe stays in the towns for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow (14:28–29), and the farmer later declares that he has given it (26:12–15). Jewish tradition harmonized the laws by counting three tithes: the Levites' tithe, a "second tithe" eaten in Jerusalem, and a tithe for the poor in the third and sixth years (Tobit 1:6–8; Mishnah Ma'aser Sheni).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 12:6, 17–18; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Deuteronomy 26:12–15; Numbers 18:21–32; Leviticus 27:30–33; Tobit 1:6–8

common: Many scholars see Deuteronomy's tithe as a reform adjusted for one central sanctuary.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 16:1–8 joins Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread and moves the sacrifice from the home, as in Exodus 12, to "the place the LORD will choose." The animal may come "from the flock and the herd," and it is to be "cooked," a word that can mean boiled, where Exodus required roasting (Exodus 12:9). Chronicles shows the tension at Josiah's Passover: "They cooked the Passover in the fire, by the rule" (2 Chronicles 35:13), combining the two laws. The unleavened bread is called "the bread of hardship," eaten because Israel came out "in a rush."
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 16:1–8; Exodus 12:1–20; 2 Kings 23:21–23; 2 Chronicles 35:1–19; Luke 2:41–42

sections.b: Deuteronomy 19:1–13 tells Israel to set apart three cities in the land, prepare roads to them, and add three more if the land grows. It gives an example of accidental killing: an axe head flies off the handle and kills a fellow woodcutter. The elders of a murderer's town must take him from the refuge city and hand him over to "the avenger of blood." Unlike Numbers 35, Deuteronomy says nothing about the death of the high priest. Moses has already named three cities east of the Jordan (4:41–43).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 4:41–43; Deuteronomy 19:1–13; Exodus 21:12–14; Numbers 35:9–34; Joshua 20

sections.b: Deuteronomy 18:10–11 gives the Bible's fullest list of forbidden practices: making a child pass through the fire, divination, reading signs, looking for omens, sorcery, casting spells, asking ghosts of the dead or spirits that know things, and seeking out the dead. All of these are called "abhorrent," and the alternative is the prophet God will raise up (18:15). Saul's visit to the woman at Endor breaks this law (1 Samuel 28), and Manasseh is condemned for nearly every item on the list (2 Kings 21:6).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 18:9–14; Leviticus 19:26, 31; Leviticus 20:6, 27; 1 Samuel 28:3–25; 2 Kings 21:6; Isaiah 8:19; Acts 16:16–18

sections.b: Deuteronomy gives two tests. A prophet whose sign comes true but who says "Let us follow other gods" must be rejected, because "the LORD your God is testing you" (13:1–5). And a word that "does not happen or come true" is a word "the LORD has not spoken" (18:22). The first test puts loyalty above miracles; the second judges predictions. Jesus warns of false prophets who will "give great signs and wonders" (Matthew 24:24), and John tells readers to "test the spirits" (1 John 4:1).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22; Jeremiah 28:9; Matthew 7:15–20; Matthew 24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 John 4:1

sections.b: Deuteronomy 25:17–19 adds a detail missing from Exodus 17: Amalek attacked Israel "when you were faint and weary" and "cut down from behind all the stragglers at your rear. He did not fear God." The command is paradoxical: remember, so that you will "wipe out the memory of Amalek from beneath the sky." Jewish synagogues read the passage on the Sabbath before Purim, linking Amalek to Haman.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Exodus 17:8–16; 1 Samuel 15; Esther 3:1

sections.b: Deuteronomy 24:19–22 adds to Leviticus' gleaning laws: a sheaf forgotten in the field must be left, and olive trees and vineyards are to be gone over only once. The leftovers belong to "the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow," and the farmer who leaves them is promised a blessing "in all the work of your hands." Another law lets a passerby eat grapes or pick grain by hand from a neighbor's field (Deuteronomy 23:24–25), the law the disciples followed in Matthew 12:1.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 23:24–25; Deuteronomy 24:19–22; Leviticus 19:9–10; Ruth 2; Matthew 12:1

sections.b: Deuteronomy 22:23–29 treats three cases. A woman promised in marriage who lies with another man in a town is presumed to have consented, "because she did not cry for help." In the open country she is presumed innocent: the case "is like a man who attacks his neighbor and murders him," and only the man dies. A man who "seizes" a virgin not promised in marriage pays her father fifty shekels, marries her and may never divorce her. Modern readers rightly question the town rule and the forced marriage; ancient and modern interpreters have narrowed both (Sifre; Ketubot 39b).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 22:23–29; Exodus 22:16–17; Genesis 34; 2 Samuel 13:1–22

common: Commentators divide on 22:28–29: many, such as Carolyn Pressler and Daniel Block, read it as seduction like Exodus 22:16, while the NIV and NRSV translate it as rape.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 12–26 is the third great collection of law in the Torah, after the Covenant Code (Exodus 20:22–23:33) and the Holiness laws (Leviticus 17–26). It reworks many older laws: the slave law (Exodus 21:2–11 in Deuteronomy 15:12–18), the feasts (Exodus 23:14–17 in Deuteronomy 16:1–17), lost animals (Exodus 23:4–5 in Deuteronomy 22:1–4) and interest (Exodus 22:25 in Deuteronomy 23:19–20). Its new themes are one place of worship, care for the poor and the Levite, and the repeated reason "remember that you were a slave in Egypt." Stephen Kaufman argued that the laws follow the order of the Ten Commandments.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 12:1–26:19; Exodus 20:22–23:33; Leviticus 17–26; 2 Kings 22:8–13

common: Most scholars link this code to the "book of the law" found in the temple under King Josiah (2 Kings 22:8).
uncommon: Some conservative scholars hold that the code goes back substantially to Moses, with later editing.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 12–26 lists many crimes punished by death: enticing others to worship other gods (13:1–18; 17:2–7), defying the high court (17:12), murder (19:11–13), the stubborn and rebellious son (21:18–21), adultery (22:22–24) and kidnapping (24:7). Most end with the formula "So you will sweep the evil out from among you." The law also limits execution: two or three witnesses are required (17:6; 19:15), the witnesses' hands must be first (17:7), and children are not to die for parents (24:16). The rabbis made executions rare: a court that executed once in seven years was called destructive, and one sage said once in seventy (Mishnah Makkot 1:10).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 13:5–11; Deuteronomy 17:2–13; Deuteronomy 19:11–21; Deuteronomy 21:18–23; Deuteronomy 22:21–24; Deuteronomy 24:7, 16; 1 Corinthians 5:13
